title: Why That Building Looks Like That
description: The gap in the sidewalk, the little holes along the bottom of a brick wall, the groove under a window ledge: buildings are covered in details that look like sloppiness and are actually load-bearing decisions. This Quiz reads a building's surface and asks what it is defending against — mostly water and temperature, which destroy buildings far more often than load does.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: A steel bridge span is 45 meters long when it is installed. Steel's linear thermal expansion coefficient is about 12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C. If the temperature rises by 30°C, about how many millimeters longer does the span become?
questions.description: Use ΔL = α × L × ΔT. Give your answer in millimeters.
questions.explanation: ΔL = (12 × 10⁻⁶ per °C) × 45,000 mm × 30°C ≈ 16.2 mm. That is a small fraction of the span's length, but it is not zero, and a 45-meter span is a short bridge — highway and rail spans run much longer. Multiply that same shift across a curtain-wall facade, a long roof deck, or a parapet coping, and a few millimeters per bay becomes centimeters across a building's length. Nothing in the structure absorbs that movement for free; a joint has to be built to take it.

questions.title: A building has expansion joints in its facade panels, its floor slabs, and its parapet coping. What job do all three shapes of joint share?

images.alt: A vertical strip running the full height between two sections of a building's stone-tiled facade, where the tiling gives way to an open metal-lined channel.
images.caption: Same building, two structural sections, one running joint between them, photographed by Hirho, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:El_G%C3%A2la_the_expansion_joint_for_separating_irregular_plan_shapes_Tenjin_1-ch%C5%8Dme_Ch%C5%AB%C5%8D-ku_Fukuoka_20251107.jpg).

options.text: Let adjoining materials expand and contract without pushing on each other
Provide a path for electrical wiring between floors
Mark the property line between two different owners
Give window washers a place to anchor equipment

questions.explanation: Whether it interrupts a facade, a slab, or a coping, an expansion joint is a deliberate break that lets each side of the building move independently with temperature and moisture, instead of transmitting that movement as stress. Without the break, two rigid sections trying to grow at slightly different rates or times can crack, bow, or spall wherever they meet. The joint is filled with a flexible material so it can open and close repeatedly without losing its seal.

questions.title: Concrete slabs almost always crack eventually as they shrink while curing and then expand and contract with temperature. What does cutting a shallow control joint into the surface accomplish, if it cannot stop the slab from cracking?

images.alt: A close-up of a broom-finished concrete surface with a straight tooled groove running diagonally across the frame; a hairline crack runs along the bottom of the groove.
images.caption: Photo by Chicagoland Concrete, Inc., CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Saw_Cut_Control_Joint_in_Concrete.jpg).

images.alt: A top-down comparison of two identical concrete slab panels: one with a scored groove where the resulting crack runs straight along it, and one with no groove where the crack wanders diagonally across the panel.
images.caption: Same slab, same shrinkage — the groove decides whether the crack is a straight hidden line or a random diagonal one.

options.text: It thins the slab along a straight line, so the crack forms there instead of at a random weak spot
It makes the concrete slightly waterproof along that line
It removes the need for reinforcing steel in the slab
It permanently welds the two sides of the slab together

questions.explanation: A control joint cuts the slab down to roughly a quarter to a third of its thickness along a chosen line. Concrete is weak in tension, so as the slab shrinks and moves, it cracks at its thinnest, weakest cross-section rather than wherever a random flaw happens to be. The crack still happens — the joint just decides where, so it lands in a straight, planned line instead of a jagged one across the middle of a panel.

questions.title: Why is a sidewalk's control-joint groove cut only shallowly into the surface, instead of all the way through the slab?

options.text: A shallow groove is enough to create a weak line for the crack to follow, while the slab underneath stays continuous enough to carry load together
Cutting deeper would make the concrete too heavy to lift
A full-depth cut would let grass grow through the sidewalk
Deeper grooves are illegal under most building codes

questions.explanation: The joint only needs to concentrate stress enough that the crack starts there rather than somewhere else; the slab does not need to be structurally separated to achieve that. A shallow groove, typically a quarter to a third of the slab's thickness, is enough to guarantee where the crack initiates while leaving most of the cross-section intact, so panels can still transfer some load to each other at the joint and the surface stays reasonably even to walk on.

questions.title: Which statements correctly explain why a very long brick wall needs a vertical movement joint somewhere along its length, while a short garden wall usually does not?

options.text: Thermal and moisture movement accumulates over distance, so a longer run of brick moves by more total millimeters than a short one
A short wall can usually absorb its small total movement in the give of ordinary mortar joints without needing a dedicated joint
Longer walls are built from a different, weaker type of brick
Short walls do not experience any temperature change

questions.explanation: Each brick and each mortar joint expands and contracts by a tiny amount, but those tiny amounts add up along the run of a wall. A wall a few meters long might move by less than a millimeter total, which the mortar can absorb without visible distress. A wall tens of meters long can accumulate enough movement to crack the brickwork or push against whatever it meets at a corner, so it needs a joint built in to take up that total movement in one place.

questions.title: A homeowner notices a crack in a plastered wall. Which description should prompt an immediate call to a structural engineer rather than a routine repaint?

options.text: A diagonal, stair-stepped crack that runs through the mortar joints near a corner and is wider at one end than the other
A thin, roughly vertical hairline crack in the paint film with no step or diagonal pattern
A crack that only appears in the paint and not in the plaster underneath
A crack that is the same width along its entire length

questions.explanation: Ordinary shrinkage and thermal movement tend to produce thin, fairly uniform, mostly vertical or horizontal cracks. A diagonal, stepped crack that follows the mortar joints and tapers — wider at one end, narrower at the other — is the signature of differential settlement or shear: one part of the foundation is moving relative to another. That pattern means load paths may be shifting, which is a structural question, not a cosmetic one.

questions.title: Why is an expansion or movement joint filled with a soft sealant or compressible foam instead of being pointed up with ordinary mortar?

images.alt: A cross-section diagram of a movement joint shown twice: narrow in summer when the surrounding material has expanded, and wide in winter when it has contracted.
images.caption: The joint's job only works if its filler can follow the gap through every season.

options.text: The whole point of the joint is to open and close with temperature, and only a flexible material can follow that movement repeatedly without cracking
Mortar is too expensive to use in a joint that thin
Sealant is a legal requirement in every country regardless of climate
Mortar cannot be colored to match the surrounding material

questions.explanation: Mortar is rigid once it cures — it can carry compression but has almost no ability to stretch. If a movement joint were pointed with mortar, the first big temperature swing would either crack the mortar or, worse, transmit the stress straight back into the adjoining panels the joint was supposed to isolate. A soft sealant or a compressible backer rod can compress in summer and stretch in winter for years, which is exactly the behavior the joint exists to provide.

questions.title: Along the bottom course of a brick veneer wall, small gaps are left in the mortar every couple of feet instead of pointing them solid. What are these gaps for?

images.alt: A close-up of a brick wall where one vertical mortar joint near the base has been left open, showing a dark gap through to the cavity behind.
images.caption: Photo by Dcorchado, CC BY-SA 4.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Weep_hole.jpg).

images.alt: A cross-section of a cavity wall showing the outer brick leaf, an air cavity with insulation, flashing sloped toward a weep hole at the base, and water draining out through the gap.
images.caption: Weep holes are the exit of a route that starts the moment rain gets past the outer brick.

options.text: They let water that has gotten into the wall cavity drain back out
They let insects nest inside the wall for pest control
They mark where the bricklayer changed batches of brick
They reduce the total weight of the wall

questions.explanation: Brick veneer is not a waterproof membrane — wind-driven rain gets through the brick face and the mortar joints regularly. The wall is built expecting that: behind the brick sits an air cavity with a drainage plane and flashing that catches the water and slopes it back outward. Weep holes are simply the open joints at the bottom of that cavity where the collected water, and the air that helps it evaporate, can leave the wall instead of soaking upward into the structure.

questions.title: In a rain screen wall system, what does keeping the cavity behind the outer cladding vented to the outside air mainly accomplish?

images.alt: A building under construction where the outer wall shows rock-wool insulation boards fixed to the structure with vertical metal support rails, with the finished cladding not yet installed.
images.caption: Before the outer panels go on, the vented cavity and its support rails are visible. Photo by Engoman23, public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Fachada_ventilada_lana_de_roca.JPG).

images.alt: A cross-section of a rain screen wall showing an outer panel, a vented air cavity, and a backup wall, with the cavity air pressure staying close to the outside wind pressure.
images.caption: A vented, open cavity keeps the air pressure inside it close to the pressure outside, which is what stops wind from driving water through the wall.

options.text: It keeps the air pressure in the cavity close to the outside pressure, so wind cannot force water through the joints in the outer skin
It lets the outer panels absorb sound from inside the building
It is only there to save material by using thinner panels
It stops the outer cladding from ever getting wet

questions.explanation: Wind does not just push rain against a wall; it also creates a pressure difference between outside air and any sealed space behind the cladding, and that pressure difference is what drives water through small gaps. A rain screen deliberately leaves the outer skin imperfectly sealed and vents the cavity behind it, so the cavity's air pressure tracks the outside pressure almost exactly. With little or no pressure difference across the outer skin's joints, wind has much less ability to force water through them, and any water that does get past drains down the vented cavity instead of being pushed further inward.

questions.title: Flashing is a thin, sloped strip of water-resistant material installed above a window or door opening in a wall. What typically happens if it is installed backward — sloped inward toward the building instead of outward — or omitted entirely?

options.text: Water that reaches that point gets directed into the wall assembly instead of away from it, often causing hidden rot or corrosion before it is ever visible
The window will not be able to open or close
The wall becomes structurally unable to carry any load
Nothing changes, because flashing is a purely decorative trim piece

questions.explanation: Flashing exists to catch water at a break in the wall's outer surface — like the top of a window opening — and route it back to the outside before it can travel further into the assembly. Because it is hidden behind trim or siding, a flashing installed backward or left out often causes no visible sign of trouble for years while water repeatedly enters the wall at that spot, rotting framing or corroding steel behind the finish. The damage is usually discovered only once it is severe, which is why flashing details get disproportionate attention in inspections relative to their size.

questions.title: A window sill has a thin groove cut into its underside, a few millimeters back from the outer edge. What does this drip groove actually stop?

images.alt: Two cross-sections of a projecting sill compared side by side: one with a plain underside where water tracks back along the surface to the wall, and one with a small groove where water drips straight down instead.
images.caption: Without a groove, surface tension carries the water film all the way back to the wall before it falls.

options.text: Water clinging to the underside of the sill and tracking back along it to run down the wall face below
Wind from lifting the window sash off its track
The sill from sagging under the weight of the window
Insects from building nests under the sill

questions.explanation: Water running off a projecting sill does not automatically fall straight down — surface tension can pull a thin film of water back along the flat underside, all the way to where the sill meets the wall, and from there it streaks or soaks the wall below. A drip groove is a small notch that breaks that surface tension: water reaching the groove cannot bridge the gap and simply drips off, clear of the wall. It is a few millimeters of stone or timber doing the job that would otherwise require a much larger overhang.

questions.title: Two identical buildings sit side by side. One has generous roof overhangs; the other has none. After ten years, which one is more likely to show heavy vertical streaking on its walls, and why?

options.text: The building with no overhangs, because rain runs directly down the full height of the facade instead of being thrown clear at the roofline
The building with overhangs, because overhangs trap moisture underneath them
Neither — overhang length has no effect on how water moves across a facade
The building with no overhangs, because it receives more direct sunlight

questions.explanation: An overhang's main weatherproofing job is simply to throw rainwater away from the wall below it, the same way a hat brim keeps rain off a collar. A wall with no overhang gets the full sheet-flow of roof runoff, plus wind-driven rain, running directly down its face for its entire height, which tends to produce visible streaking, more frequent wetting cycles, and faster weathering of the material. A generous overhang breaks that path near the top, so much less water ever reaches the wall face at all.

questions.title: A white, powdery bloom appears on the surface of an exterior brick wall. What is efflorescence actually telling you about the wall?

options.text: Moisture has been moving through the masonry and dissolved salts are being left behind on the surface as the water evaporates
The bricks were fired at too low a temperature during manufacturing
The wall has been painted with the wrong type of paint
Mold is growing on the brick surface

questions.explanation: Efflorescence forms when water moving through masonry or concrete dissolves naturally occurring salts in the material, carries them to the surface, and then evaporates, leaving the salts behind as a white crust. The bloom itself is usually harmless and can often be brushed off, but it is a symptom, not the underlying problem — it means water is finding a way through the wall, and the real question is where that water is entering and whether it is a one-time event or an ongoing leak worth tracing.

questions.title: In cold climates, why does saturated masonry or concrete paving tend to flake and crumble at its surface after repeated winters, even without any change in load?

options.text: Water trapped in the material's pores expands as it freezes, and the repeated pressure eventually breaks small pieces off the surface
Cold temperatures make concrete chemically dissolve over time
Snow is slightly acidic and etches the surface of the material
Low temperatures cause the internal steel reinforcement to shrink and pull away from the concrete

questions.explanation: Water expands by roughly nine percent when it freezes. If masonry, concrete, or stone is saturated and then freezes, that expansion happens inside the material's pores and small cracks, generating internal pressure with nowhere to go. One freeze cycle rarely does visible damage, but repeated freeze-thaw cycles over many winters progressively weaken the surface until small flakes or larger chunks break away — a failure mode called freeze-thaw spalling, driven entirely by water and temperature rather than by any structural load.

questions.title: In traditional masonry, mortar is deliberately made softer and weaker than the brick or stone units it holds together. Why is that the goal, rather than a compromise?

options.text: If something has to crack or wear from movement and weathering, a weaker mortar joint fails first and can be repaired, instead of the brick or stone itself cracking
Weak mortar is simply cheaper to produce than strong mortar
Strong mortar would make the wall too heavy to build safely
Building codes require mortar to be the weakest material in any masonry wall

questions.explanation: Mortar is a sacrificial layer by design. Small movements from thermal cycling, settlement, and moisture are inevitable in a masonry wall, and something in the assembly has to absorb them. If mortar is softer than the surrounding brick or stone, it takes that stress and, over decades, develops hairline cracking or gradual erosion — both of which can be repaired by repointing, replacing only the mortar. If the mortar were harder than the masonry units, the same stress would instead crack the brick or stone itself, which is far more difficult and expensive to fix.

questions.title: Why can repointing old, soft-lime brickwork with modern, hard Portland cement mortar actually accelerate damage to the brick, instead of fixing the wall?

options.text: The harder mortar no longer serves as the sacrificial layer, so movement and moisture-driven stress get pushed into the older, softer brick instead, where it causes cracking or spalling
Portland cement mortar is toxic to the clay used in older bricks
Modern mortar cannot physically bond to brick manufactured before the twentieth century
Cement mortar is always a different color, which weakens the wall aesthetically but not structurally

questions.explanation: Historic brick and lime mortar were designed as a matched pair, with the mortar softer and more porous than the brick, so the mortar absorbed movement and let moisture evaporate outward. Modern Portland cement mortar is much harder and less permeable. Repointing old brickwork with it flips the sacrificial relationship: now the mortar is stronger than the brick, so seasonal movement stresses the brick instead, and trapped moisture that can no longer evaporate through the mortar pushes outward through the brick face, contributing to spalling. Matching mortar hardness to the masonry it repairs is a standard heritage-conservation principle for exactly this reason.

questions.title: The coping stones or metal caps along the top of a parapet wall are almost always installed with a slight slope and an overhanging drip edge, rather than sitting perfectly flat and flush. Which statements correctly explain why?

options.text: The slope sheds rainwater off the top of the wall instead of letting it pond and soak downward into the parapet
An overhanging edge with a drip detail flings shedding water clear of the wall face below, the same principle as a sill
It reduces the total amount of material needed to cap the wall
It is purely a historical style convention with no functional purpose today

questions.explanation: A parapet's coping is the most exposed, most saturated part of the wall — it takes rain directly from above with nothing overhead to shield it. A perfectly flat cap would let water pond on top and slowly work its way down into the masonry through any hairline crack or joint, so the coping is sloped, usually toward the roof side or with a slight camber, to shed that water quickly. The same coping typically also projects past the wall face with a drip edge underneath, so the water it sheds falls clear of the wall instead of running down and streaking it — the sill's drip groove at parapet scale. Together, these are a major reason well-detailed parapets outlast poorly detailed ones even when built from the same materials.

questions.title: Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, so steel reinforcing bars are placed wherever tension is expected. In a simply supported beam that sags under load, and in a cantilever that projects from a single support, where does the rebar mostly sit?

options.text: Near the bottom of a simply supported beam, where sagging puts the concrete into tension
Near the top of a cantilever, where the projecting arm puts the upper concrete into tension
Rebar placement does not depend on which side of the concrete is in tension
Rebar is placed at the exact center of every concrete section regardless of the loading case

questions.explanation: The rule is the same in both cases: put the steel where the concrete would otherwise be pulled apart. A simply supported beam sags downward under load, which stretches the bottom fibers, so the main reinforcement runs near the bottom. A cantilever bends the opposite way — it curves so the top fibers stretch and the bottom fibers compress — so its main reinforcement runs near the top. Reversing the two, or centering the steel, would leave the tension zone essentially unreinforced and prone to cracking.

questions.title: Building codes specify a minimum thickness of concrete, called cover, between the outer surface of a concrete member and the reinforcing steel inside it. Why is too little cover classified as a durability problem rather than a strength problem?

images.alt: A side-by-side comparison of two concrete cross-sections: one with a rebar well embedded beneath an intact concrete surface, and one with a shallow, rusted, expanded rebar that has cracked and spalled the surface above it.
images.caption: Cover that is too shallow does not make the beam weaker on day one — it makes the steel inside it start rusting years sooner.

options.text: The concrete itself still carries the same load either way; thin cover instead lets moisture, chlorides, or carbon dioxide reach the steel sooner and start corrosion earlier
Thin cover immediately reduces the concrete's ability to resist compression
Cover thickness only affects the finished appearance of the concrete surface
Cover requirements exist only to make room for architectural finishes

questions.explanation: On the day a member is cast, a few millimeters of extra or missing cover barely changes its load-carrying capacity — the concrete section and the steel are both still there. What cover really controls is how long it takes for water, dissolved chlorides, or carbonation from the air to reach the steel and start it corroding. Once corrosion begins, it eventually cracks and spalls the concrete off from the inside, which is when a durability problem finally becomes a strength problem, often decades after construction. That long delay between cause and visible failure is exactly why minimum cover is treated as a strict, non-negotiable code requirement rather than a nice-to-have.

questions.title: A parking garage ceiling has a patch of concrete flaking away, revealing rusted rebar underneath. What mechanism is directly responsible for pushing that chunk of concrete off?

images.alt: A concrete building wall where a section of the surface has broken away in a line, exposing several corroded, rust-streaked steel reinforcing bars underneath.
images.caption: Photo by Cullen328 (Jim Heaphy), CC BY-SA 3.0, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Concrete_spalling_caused_by_oxide_jacking_at_the_Herbst_Pavilion,_Fort_Mason_Center,_San_Francisco.jpg).

options.text: Rust occupies several times the volume of the original steel, and that expansion physically pushes the surrounding concrete apart from the inside
The weight of parked cars directly crushes the concrete at that spot
The rebar dissolves completely, leaving a hollow void that the ceiling collapses into
Rust makes the concrete around it chemically brittle without any change in volume

questions.explanation: Iron oxide, the product of steel corroding, takes up substantially more volume than the metallic steel it replaces. As rust forms on an embedded bar, it has nowhere to expand except outward into the surrounding concrete, generating pressure the concrete was never designed to resist from the inside. That pressure eventually cracks and delaminates the cover, popping pieces of concrete loose in a process often called rust jacking or oxide jacking — a purely volumetric, mechanical effect, not a chemical weakening of the concrete itself. Parking garages and coastal structures see this often because road salt and marine air both accelerate the underlying corrosion.

questions.title: Which environments tend to make reinforced concrete structures deteriorate fastest, and why?

options.text: Parking garages exposed to de-icing road salt tracked in on vehicle tires
Coastal balconies and structures exposed to airborne sea salt
Chloride ions accelerate steel corrosion once they reach the reinforcing bar
Dry inland environments with no salt exposure age reinforced concrete fastest

questions.explanation: Chloride ions — from de-icing salt tracked into parking garages or from airborne salt spray near the coast — are especially damaging because they break down the passive protective layer that normally forms on steel embedded in concrete's alkaline environment, letting corrosion start even where cover thickness would otherwise be adequate. That is why parking structures and coastal buildings are disproportionately represented in concrete durability failures compared with similar structures in dry, salt-free inland environments, even when they were built to the same original strength.

questions.title: How does carbonation, the slow reaction between carbon dioxide in the air and concrete, eventually lead to reinforcing steel corroding, even without any chloride exposure?

options.text: Carbonation lowers the concrete's internal pH over time, and once it reaches the steel, the steel loses the protective passive layer that high alkalinity normally maintains
Carbonation physically dissolves the steel bars directly
Carbonation increases the concrete's alkalinity, which speeds up corrosion
Carbonation only affects the color of the concrete surface, not its chemistry near the steel

questions.explanation: Fresh concrete is highly alkaline, and that alkalinity keeps embedded steel covered in a thin, stable, passive oxide film that resists corrosion — the same reason cover thickness matters so much. Over years, carbon dioxide from the air slowly reacts with the concrete near the surface and reduces its pH, in a process called carbonation, working its way inward like a front. Once that carbonation front reaches the depth of the reinforcing steel, the alkalinity there drops enough that the passive film breaks down, and ordinary corrosion can begin even in a structure that was never exposed to chlorides.

questions.title: A concrete beam shows a thin, reddish-brown streak running down its face from a hairline crack, with no visible spalling yet. What does that stain most likely indicate to an inspector?

options.text: Corrosion has already started on reinforcing steel somewhere near that crack, and the rust is bleeding out through the crack before any concrete has broken away
The concrete mix originally contained too much sand
The stain is always just surface dirt with no connection to the concrete's internal condition
The beam was painted with a low-quality sealant that is now failing

questions.explanation: A rust-colored streak on an otherwise intact concrete surface is a strong diagnostic sign, not a coincidence — the color comes from iron oxide, which forms specifically where embedded steel is corroding. Because that streak often appears before enough pressure has built up to spall the cover off, it functions as an early warning: the corrosion process described by chloride exposure, carbonation, and rust jacking is already underway beneath the surface, even though the concrete there hasn't visibly broken yet. Inspectors treat these stains as a cue to investigate further, not just repaint over.

questions.title: On the face of some concrete parking structures and bridge decks, a regular grid of circular or square patches is visible, slightly different in texture from the surrounding concrete. What do these patches typically mark?

options.text: The anchors where post-tensioning cables were stressed and locked off after the concrete cured, then patched over
Decorative tile that has since fallen off
Random repair work with no relationship to the structure's design
Ventilation ports for curing the concrete during construction

questions.explanation: Post-tensioned concrete contains steel cables or tendons that run through ducts cast into the member and are stressed — pulled tight — after the concrete has gained strength, putting the concrete into beneficial compression. That stressing happens at anchorages, fittings at the ends of each cable where the tension is locked in. Once the cable is tensioned and cut, the anchorage pocket is patched with new concrete or grout, which is why a regular grid of slightly different-textured patches across a post-tensioned deck or wall usually marks exactly where those anchors sit.

questions.title: On the ceiling of an older building, faint dark lines sometimes appear running parallel to hidden structural elements below the surface, like joists or slab edges. What causes this pattern, sometimes called ghosting?

images.alt: A cross-section of a wall showing a structural stud running through the insulation layer, next to a comparison view of an interior surface with a darker strip of dust buildup directly over where that stud sits.
images.caption: The stud conducts heat faster than the insulation around it, so the surface above it runs colder — and colder surfaces collect airborne dust faster.

options.text: The structural element conducts heat faster than the surrounding insulation, so the surface above it runs slightly colder and collects airborne dust faster over time
The structural element is leaking a small amount of oil that stains the surface
The pattern is caused by uneven paint application during the original construction
The lines mark where electrical wiring runs beneath the surface

questions.explanation: This is thermal bridging made visible. A stud, joist, or slab edge typically conducts heat much faster than the insulation around it, so the interior surface directly above or in front of it sits at a slightly lower temperature than the rest of the wall or ceiling. Airborne dust tends to deposit somewhat faster onto cooler surfaces, so over months and years that temperature difference slowly builds a visible line of dust — ghosting — that traces the hidden structure underneath even though nothing is actually leaking or unevenly painted.

questions.title: Modern glass office towers often have windows with a faint blue, green, or bronze color cast when viewed from outside, even though the glass looks clear from indoors. Which statements correctly explain this?

options.text: A low-emissivity coating, applied to reflect infrared heat while passing visible light, is the most common cause of the cast
Different low-e coating formulations reflect light slightly differently, which is why one tower reads bronze and another reads blue
The glass has been tinted for privacy and blocks most visible light
It indicates the glass is structurally weaker than untinted glass

questions.explanation: Low-emissivity, or low-e, coatings are microscopically thin metallic or metal-oxide layers applied to glass to reflect infrared radiation — reducing unwanted heat gain or loss — while still letting most visible light through. Different coating formulations interact with light slightly differently, which is why one building's glass reads faintly blue and another's reads bronze or green from the outside, even though both perform a similar energy function and both look nearly clear from indoors where the reflection angle is different.

questions.title: On a glass curtain-wall tower, the vision glass at each floor is bordered above and below by an opaque strip of glass or metal in roughly the same color family. What is behind that opaque strip?

options.text: The edge of the floor slab and the structure at that level, along with any mechanical elements, which the opaque spandrel panel is hiding from view
Nothing — it is solid glass all the way through with no structure behind it
A separate, unoccupied mechanical floor between every occupied floor
Decorative trim with no relationship to the building's structure

questions.explanation: A curtain wall's vision glass gives occupants a view out at eye level, but the building's actual floor slabs, perimeter beams, and sometimes ductwork or fire-stopping have to go somewhere at each level — usually right behind the strip between one floor's vision glass and the next. Spandrel panels, made opaque with an internal coating, insulation backing, or metal facing, cover that structural and mechanical zone so the facade reads as continuous glass from outside while hiding the parts of the building nobody needs to see.

questions.title: Why do many modern facades include a visible horizontal shadow gap or reveal at each floor line, rather than a perfectly flush surface from top to bottom?

options.text: It commonly conceals a construction or movement joint between floor-by-floor sections of the facade, while also giving the surface a deliberate visual reveal
It is required so window washers have a place to stand
It marks the floor line for firefighters approaching from outside
It has no relationship to how the facade is actually constructed

questions.explanation: Many facade systems are erected and finished floor by floor, and the horizontal line where one story's cladding meets the next is a natural place for a small joint that accommodates construction tolerances, deflection of the floor slab under load, and thermal movement, all without visibly cracking a continuous surface. Detailing that line as a deliberate shadow gap or reveal turns a functional necessity into part of the facade's rhythm — the line has to exist structurally either way, so architects design it rather than trying to hide it.

questions.title: In older, pre-steel-frame masonry buildings, the walls are often noticeably thicker at the ground floor than near the roof. Which statements correctly explain why?

options.text: In load-bearing masonry, every floor's wall has to carry the weight of all the floors and roof above it, so the accumulated load is greatest at the bottom
Unreinforced masonry has a roughly fixed compressive strength per unit of cross-sectional area, so carrying more accumulated load requires more wall thickness
Thicker walls at the base were purely a decorative fashion with no structural reason
Ground floors are thicker only to resist flooding, not to carry load

questions.explanation: Before steel and reinforced-concrete frames took over load-bearing duty, masonry walls themselves had to carry every floor's weight straight down to the foundation. A wall near the roof only supports the roof; a wall at the ground floor supports the roof plus every floor below it, so it carries far more compressive load. Because unreinforced masonry's compressive strength is roughly fixed per unit of cross-sectional area, resisting that larger accumulated load required more material — thicker walls — lower in the building, tapering thinner toward the top where the accumulated load is smallest.
